    How the check works

    Most strength meters count character types and length. That rates P@ssw0rd1! as strong, though cracking tools guess it in seconds. FortiPass instead looks for the cheapest way to describe your password piece by piece, the way an attacker's rules engine does:

    • Dictionary words in English and Czech — also glued together, as in correcthorse, and with accents removed — plus very common passwords and names.
    • Predictable swaps such as @ for a, 0 for o and 1 for i or l.
    • Years and dates, repeated characters, keyboard and alphabet runs (qwertz, 4321) and copies of an earlier part (Ab3$Ab3$).

    Each piece costs as many bits as it would take to guess, and the cheapest split wins. The result is shown as entropy in bits and as an average crack time for an offline attack at 100 billion guesses per second — the same assumption as the crack-time table.

    What it cannot know

    No checker can know your pet's name, your street or the password you used in 2014. More importantly, it cannot tell whether a password has already leaked: a leaked password is cracked in zero seconds, however long it is. Checking that needs a database of breaches, which this page deliberately never contacts. Use Have I Been Pwned for that, and read a good score here as “no obvious weakness found”, not as a guarantee.

    Turn a weak password into a strong one

    • Make it longer before you make it more complicated — length multiplies the search space fastest.
    • Replace anything you made up with something random: a generated passphrase if you have to type it, a random password if a password manager fills it in.
    • Use it on one site only. Reuse is how one breach turns into many.

    Questions people ask

    Is it safe to type my real password here?

    The check runs entirely in your browser and the page's Content Security Policy blocks every network request, so nothing can be sent. Still, be wary of typing real passwords into any website — if in doubt, disconnect from the internet first, or test a password with the same structure instead.

    Why does my password with symbols and numbers score low?

    Because the checker sees through the usual tricks. A dictionary word with a capital letter, a year and an exclamation mark is a pattern that cracking tools try in the first minutes. Length and genuine randomness are what make a password strong.

    What does the crack time assume?

    An attacker who has stolen a database of password hashes and makes 100 billion guesses per second — realistic for fast hashes such as MD5 or NTLM on a multi-GPU rig. It is the average time, half the search space. Sites using bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 make attacks far slower, and a login form with rate limiting slower still.

    Does it check whether my password was in a data breach?

    No — that would mean sending something over the network, which FortiPass never does. Have I Been Pwned offers a breach check that only receives the first five characters of your password's SHA-1 hash.

    Why do different checkers give different results?

    They assume different attackers (guesses per second, hash type) and different models of how passwords are made; many only count character classes. Compare the reasoning, not just the number.
